ImageDescription.value: Bhai-dooj is another festival which celebrates the love of brother and sister. It is celebrated on 2nd day after Diwali. It falls on the last day of 5-days long Diwali festival (1st day - dhanteras, 2nd day- narkachaudas/narak chaturdashi/chhoti diwali, 3rd day- diwali/deepawali, 4th day- Govardhan pooja/Annakut, 5th day- bhai-dooj/bhai-tilak/bhai-beej). It is a Hindu festival. As per the anecdotes, this festival is inspired from the brother-sister love between yamraj (king of yam-lok) and yamuna. On this occasion, sisters pray to goddess Yamuna for happy, healthy and long life of their brothers. They do the tilak-ceremony (which includes application of long tilak on brother's forehead along with rice and giving dry coconut along with "doob", a type of grass) and offer sweets to their brothers. In return, brothers also offers sweets and other gifts.

After moving up country they joined the force under Sir James Outram at the Alumbagh near Lucknow in February 1858. The following month they took part in the final capture of that city. ImageDescription.value: Following the outbreak of the Indian Mutiny (1857-1859), the 7th (The Queen's Own) Regiment of (Light) Dragoons (Hussars) were sent from Britain to the subcontinent, arriving at Madras in November 1857. After moving up country they joined the force under Sir James Outram at the Alumbagh near Lucknow in February 1858. The following month they took part in the final capture of that city. The 7th then formed part of Sir James Hope Grant's column engaged in defeating the last of the rebels. Following the end of the rising the regiment remained in India until 1871.

ImageDescription.value:
A One Hundred Dollar Confederate States of America banknote dated December 22, 1862. Issued during the American Civil War (1861–1865).

Slave hoeing cotton in the center with John C. Calhoun on the left and Columbia on the right. Over 670,000 of these notes were issued from August, 1862 to January, 1863. [1]

The bill is 7.375 by 3.125 inches (187 mm by 79 mm) and is thinner than a modern US dollar.

Annotations on the banknote.

Serial number 131615
Keatinge & Ball, Columbia, S.C. (lower left)
Receivable in Payment of All Dues Except Export Duties. (lower right)
Issued by Maj. James Glover, q.m. 26th January 1863 (hand written on back)
Interest Paid to 1st January 1864 at Richmond. (stamped on back) The ink from this stamp can be seen on the front right side.

Categories.value: Self-published work|Sirr al-Maktum

ImageDescription.value:
The Sirr al-Maktum (The Hidden Secret) is a Mughal manuscript held in the Raza Library, Rampur. It illustrates a thirteenth-century Arabic text on astral magic by the Persian scholar Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, written for an unnamed king. The original treatise describes talismanic practices, astral invocations, and divinatory rituals drawn from a wide variety of traditions, situating it within the broader occult sciences of the medieval Islamic world. 
A Persian translation was produced around 1580 CE at Akbar’s imperial workshop, where its many folios were illustrated according to the zodiac, each sign paired with talismanic imagery believed to channel astral power. The manuscript carries the seal of Asaf ud-Daula, Nawab of Awadh, suggesting that it became a part of his collection during the late Mughal period. Several of its folios remain in a vulnerable condition, underscoring the importance of digital preservation.
